doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Expulsion from school, Juilliard scholarship and immigrant parents
summary: Gibbs was thrown out of school for hitting a teacher and turned down a Juilliard scholarship; talks of his Russian-speaking parents and touring at 12 with Major Bowes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Monday at 2:00? Yes I do. All right. Thank you. Bye. I have an appointment. You know it’s the only time I ever leave my house is to go to a doctor’s office. I sit here most of the time and watch, I’m a big sports nut so I watch a lot of, I bought myself a 75” TV set and I get as close to it as I can so I feel like I’m sitting in the stadium.

Well let me tell you. I got thrown out of school for hitting a teacher. You read that. Right? I hit a teacher and unbeknownst to me the bandleader and the orchestra leader came to my house to tell my folks that if I came back and apologized to the teacher, the principal and the whole classroom that they were going to give me the scholarship to Juilliard as a snare drummer and tympanist. You know in school, when you get into the percussion section you start out with the triangle because there’s a tympanist who’s a senior and gradually you graduate to the cymbals and you graduate to maybe another instrument like the snare drum. That’s like second highest. And if you’re that good you get to be the tympanist. And so they would give me the scholarship to Juilliard. In those days you couldn’t get into Juilliard without a scholarship. It wasn’t the school that it became later on where it became that — it was a school that a guy like Tony Scott, that’s where I first heard him, at Juilliard. But I didn’t want to go back to school and my folks, they knew where I was going sort of, musically, and so they didn’t force me to go back. My folks were very understanding people in the way, their way of living was completely different than I was. I was an American, they still had that foreign thing in their system. They spoke Russian, Yiddish, and they were learning — my father spoke fairly decent English and I mentioned in my book where my mother learned how to speak English from a black janitor next door, and she sounded, she got to sound too hip for the neighborhood because she would say, “Hey man” or who knows what he was saying, but my mother would talk to me and I said who am I speaking with? One of the guys on 52nd Street. I didn’t know what she was saying. But anyhow they were understanding people and they, and of course by that time, after I got out, I didn’t want to go back but then I went on the road with bands playing drums. So they saw that and as a result since I was 12 years old, when I was 12 I went on the road with Major Bowes. I was a very talented, I was a child prodigy sort of, really. And so instrumentally I had the xylophones down, really had it down. I could play anything.
